The barocaloric effect of liquid crystal is proposed for cooling applications.
Liquid crystal needs a low pressure of tens of MPa to induce the phase transition.
The barocaloric temperature change in liquid crystal is around 3 K for a pressure variation of 40 MPa.
The barocaloric strength of liquid crystal can be up to 75 K/GPa, much larger than current barocaloric materials (4-15 K/GPa).
The transition temperature of liquid crystal can be tuned from -2.1°C to 55.6°C by changing the acyl chain length from 12 to 18 carbons.
The entropy change of liquid crystal increases from 40 J/K/kg to 200 J/K/kg as the acyl chain length increases from 12 to 18 carbons.
The pressure dependence of the transition temperature, dT/dP, is around 0.2 K/MPa for liquid crystal.
Compared to other mechanocaloric materials, liquid crystal has a similar stress requirement, larger volumetric entropy change, and larger mass entropy change than most solid materials.
Liquid crystal exhibits a fast dynamic response to pressure oscillations at 1 Hz, indicating potential for high-frequency cooling applications.

The advantages of liquid crystal over solid caloric materials include solving the position conflict between pressure and heat exchange, no breakage problem, and potential for direct replacement of gas coolants in vapor compression refrigerators.

Potential future research directions include further investigation of liquid crystal for cooling, exploring multi-caloric effects, and investigating biological systems like deep-sea bacteria for self-healing refrigeration.
The barocaloric effect in liquid crystal is attributed to the transition between the lamellar liquid crystal (Lα) and lamellar gel (Lβ') phases.
The liquid crystal used in the study is dihexadecylphosphatidylethanolamine (DHPE) in excess water.
The high transition temperature of 82°C for DHPE limits its near room temperature cooling application.
The transition temperature and entropy change of liquid crystal can be tuned by adjusting the acyl chain length and applied pressure.
